newsitem.title: USA: Clinton declares Mexico has will to fight drugs.
newsitem.headline: Clinton declares Mexico has will to fight drugs.

text.p: U.S. President Bill Clinton on Saturday defended his decision to declare Mexico a U.S. partner in the war on drugs, praising President Ernesto Zedillo for his "brave action" in a tough battle that must be fought together.
"Make no mistake about it, Mexico has a serious drug problem," Clinton said in his weekly radio address. "But Mexico's leaders recognise that problem and they have the will to fight it."

Clinton sidestepped confrontation with a key neighbour and trade partner in certifying Mexico as an ally in the fight against drugs, but set the stage for a domestic political challenge from Congress.

His decision on Friday brought a barrage of criticism from Democratic colleagues, including Sen. Dianne Feinstein of California who is leading an effort to overturn the ruling, as well as opposition Republicans.
But Clinton said on Saturday the United States must give Mexico the means to succeed.

"Mexican President Zedillo is fighting a tough, uphill battle against the drug cartels which corrupt Mexico's law enforcement agencies. But President Zedillo has taken brave action," he said, citing the firing of 1,200 officials, extradition of criminals for the first time, passage of tough laws, and the arrest of his own drug czar for corruption.
"Stamping out the drug trade is a long-term battle, it won't be won overnight ... this is a battle we must fight together with other nations," Clinton said.
He added, however, that the United States would continue to press Mexico to take tough action against drugs.
But many members of Congress were not mollified by the reasoning behind the Clinton administration's certification of Mexico.

"I don't think it's the right decision," declared Representative Richard Gephardt of Missouri, the Democratic leader in the House of Representatives. Democratic Sen. John Kerry of Massachusetts said certification sent the wrong signal to Mexico and raised questions about the seriousness of U.S. efforts to fight drugs.
Republicans were even less kind, calling Clinton soft on drugs and warning of an erosion of support for Mexico.

"Certifying that Mexico is cooperating with the United States in the war on drugs is, in a word, a fraud," said North Carolina Republican Jesse Helms, the powerful chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee.

"Certification sends a message to those officials who are in bed with the drug lords that the United States is not serious ... the American people must pray that this decision will not stand," he said.

At least 40 of the 100 U.S. senators signed a letter to Clinton this week urging him to decertify Mexico because of widespread government corruption. Criticism in Congress was fuelled by the embarrassing arrest last week of Mexico's anti-narcotics chief Gen. Jesus Gutierrez Rebollo for allegedly taking bribes from a drug kingpin.

Nevertheless, Clinton went ahead with certification on the advice of his foreign policy team who argued that to do anything else would only have made it even harder to win Mexico's cooperation in the war on drugs.
"To decertify Mexico would just weaken President (Ernesto) Zedillo just as he is fighting to weed out corruption among officials in his government," one official said.
Apart from the diplomatic ignominy, failure to be certified also can lead to harsh U.S. economic and trade sanctions.

Congress faces a tough task in its efforts to reverse the president's decision. A resolution would have to be passed by both the House and the Senate within 30 days and sent to Clinton for his signature.
He would almost certainly veto it, automatically returning it to Congress where it would have to approved again by a two-thirds majority in order to become effective.
